title: The Second Voyage of Sindbad the Sailor

explainer.heading: The story in brief
explainer.body: Sindbad falls asleep on a beautiful uninhabited island and his ship leaves without him. He escapes by tying himself to a giant bird, the rukh, lands in a valley of diamonds full of serpents, and escapes again by hiding under a carcass carried off by a vulture. Merchants rescue him and he shares his diamonds.
explainer.example: Theme: courage, presence of mind and luck.

explainer.heading: Stranded
explainer.body: The island had ripe fruit, birds of bright plumage, rare flowers and clear streams. The breeze and murmuring stream lulled him to sleep; when he woke, the ship was far out at sea. Climbing a tree, he saw a huge white dome about fifty paces round with no door.

explainer.heading: The rukh
explainer.body: The sky darkened — not a cloud but a monstrous bird blotting out the sun. Sindbad remembered travellers’ stories of the rukh, which fed its young on elephants: the dome was its egg. When the bird slept on the egg, he twisted his turban into a rope, tied himself to its foot, and next morning it carried him to a tableland. It then flew off with a huge serpent in its talons.

explainer.heading: The valley of diamonds
explainer.body: The valley floor was strewn with large diamonds, with gigantic serpents coiled among them. A carcass fell before him, reminding him of a merchant’s story: merchants throw slaughtered animals into the valley; diamonds stick to them; vultures carry them up to the mountain, where the merchants scare the birds away and collect the diamonds.

explainer.heading: Escape and sharing
explainer.body: Sindbad filled his clothes with diamonds, tied himself under a carcass (the stench was horrible) and a vulture carried him to a ledge near the summit. A merchant scared the bird away and was disappointed to find no diamonds — so Sindbad promised him ten diamond pieces. The merchants praised his bravery.
explainer.example: “Don’t worry dear merchant! I shall give you ten diamond pieces!”

explainer.heading: Vocabulary
explainer.body: uninhabited (no people live there), plumage (feathers), slumber (sleep), circumference (distance around), carcass (dead body of an animal), talons (claws), stench (bad smell). Phrasal verbs with through / on: go through (experience), get through (survive/pass), carry on (continue), hold on (wait/grip).

explainer.heading: Grammar: passive tenses (review)
explainer.body: Passive = be (in the right tense) + past participle. The object becomes the subject; “by” shows the doer.
explainer.example: Active: A vulture carried the carcass. → Passive: The carcass was carried by a vulture. / Diamonds are found in the valley. / Sindbad has been rescued.

explainer.heading: Writing: a book review
explainer.body: Title and author, genre, brief plot (no spoilers), characters, what you liked/disliked, your rating and recommendation.

questions.q: How did Sindbad end up stranded on the island?
questions.model: He sat admiring the beautiful island; the soft breeze and murmuring stream lulled him to sleep. When he woke, his ship had sailed far out into the ocean, leaving him alone.

questions.q: What does Sindbad’s promise to the merchant show about him?
questions.model: It shows he was generous and kind-hearted. He felt sorry for the disappointed merchant and promised him ten diamond pieces, showing he believed in sharing.
points: Felt sorry for the merchant; promised ten diamonds

questions.q: Write a character sketch of Sindbad with examples from the story.
questions.model: Sindbad is adventurous and brave — he faces the giant rukh, serpents and vultures. He is quick-thinking: he twists his turban into a rope to tie himself to the rukh, and remembers the merchants’ trick to escape by hiding under a carcass despite the stench. He is calm in danger and observant, recognising the egg and the bird from travellers’ stories. He is generous, promising ten diamonds to the disappointed merchant. Luck also favours him.
